current_public_observation.visible_positioning: This is a minimalist, chic, and fast starting point. Use the navigation above to explore the site.
current_public_observation.diagnosis: The current public homepage reads as a starter shell and does not communicate the actual practice, body of work, project scale, or differentiated production systems.

north_star.core_positioning: This is not ordinary graphic design. CBenton builds coded visual systems that turn a project into an expandable campaign, publication, edition, or family of coordinated artifacts.
north_star.primary_value_proposition: Make ambitious projects look larger, more complete, more official, more collectible, and more visually coherent without reducing the work to a single isolated graphic.
north_star.business_model: Project-based custom work, campaign systems, publication systems, selected experimental commissions, consulting, workflow integration, and potential licensing.
do_not_position_as: a storefront menu of isolated deliverables

practice_model.description: The portfolio should show that individual outputs are instances of larger systems. A ticket, poster, handout, PDF, mailing piece, glyph, or webpage is often one node in a repeatable architecture.
recurring_capabilities: visual identity applied across families of outputs

examples: player-specific ticket systems with unique names, jersey data, origin logic, barcodes, sigils, and one-of-one presentation
edition structures with deterministic marks, identifiers, issue logic, and provenance cues

hero.eyebrow: CODED VISUAL SYSTEMS / CAMPAIGN PRODUCTION / PUBLICATION ARCHITECTURE
hero.headline: I build visual systems, not isolated graphics.
hero.subhead: Campaigns, editions, publications, print systems, and serialized visual objects designed to expand—so a small project can arrive with the presence of a much larger one.

sections.heading: One project. A whole visual system.
sections.copy: A project may begin with one artifact, but the work is designed to extend: posters, PDFs, print pieces, sequences, editions, identifiers, mailers, launch materials, or other coordinated outputs can grow from the same underlying visual logic.

sections.heading: Selected systems
sections.presentation: Large visual case-study cards with system name, short premise, number/types of outputs, and one sentence explaining the rule set.

sections.heading: Built with rules, not templates.
sections.copy: Many projects use custom layout logic, variable data, deterministic marks, edition structures, print constraints, or generative rules. The result is repeatable without becoming generic.

sections.heading: Project-based by design.
sections.copy: Engagements are scoped around the system a project needs—not around an hourly menu of isolated design tasks.

sections.heading: For teams that need the system, not just the output.
sections.copy: Available for selected consulting, workflow integration, collaboration, and licensing conversations where the production method itself has value.

avoid: a flat masonry gallery with no explanation
categories such as logo / flyer / brochure as the primary hierarchy
thumbnail grids that make system work look like unrelated single pieces

required_sections.heading: What changes from unit to unit
required_sections.purpose: Make serialization, data variation, provenance, geometry, color, glyphs, or other controlled differences legible.

required_sections.heading: What the system makes possible
required_sections.purpose: Explain the project advantage: scale, consistency, speed, identity, collectibility, official presence, or repeatable production.

pricing_page.page_strategy: Replace service-menu pricing with project-shaped engagement types. The page should explain how projects are scoped and what kinds of systems can be commissioned. Do not invent dollar figures unless the repository already contains approved amounts.

hero.headline: Pricing follows the system, not the number of mouse clicks.
hero.copy: Most work is quoted as a project. Scope depends on how many outputs the system needs to generate, how much variation is built in, how much production logic is required, and whether the work is a finished campaign, a reusable framework, or both.

engagements.name: Focused Project
engagements.best_for: A clearly defined visual problem that still benefits from a coherent system rather than a one-off treatment.

engagements.name: Campaign System
engagements.best_for: Projects that need multiple coordinated assets and a visual logic that can expand across a launch, event, release, artist project, or public campaign.
engagements.scope_language: Quoted from campaign scope, number of asset families, production complexity, and rollout needs.

engagements.name: Serialized / Variable Edition System
engagements.best_for: Work where each unit should be related but not identical.
engagements.scope_language: Quoted from the number of variables, number of units, rule complexity, proofing requirements, and final production format.

engagements.name: Publication / Document System
engagements.best_for: Dense information that needs a designed architecture rather than ordinary document formatting.
engagements.scope_language: Quoted from page count, information density, diagram requirements, source condition, and print/digital outputs.

engagements.name: Workflow Integration / Consulting
engagements.best_for: Studios, agencies, teams, or collaborators interested in the production method itself.
engagements.scope_language: Professional consulting engagement; scope defined before work begins.

engagements.name: Selective Small Projects
engagements.best_for: Unusual, ambitious, culturally interesting, visually strange, or genuinely compelling projects that do not fit a larger engagement.
examples: artist or community project with strong fit
engagements.scope_language: Accepted selectively. Small budget does not automatically mean discounted work.

quote_factors: number of unique or variable units
amount of custom rule / layout development
whether the client receives a reusable system in addition to final outputs
pricing_copy_rules: Do not lead with hourly rates.
Do not price every artifact separately.
Do not frame custom code, automation, or variable production as a free add-on.
Do not publish invented starting prices.
If approved prices already exist in repository content, preserve the numbers but reorganize them under project engagements.
The page should make clear that serious consulting, integration, and licensing conversations are distinct from ordinary small design requests.

approach_page.headline: Design the rule set. Then let the project expand.

sections.heading: 1. Define the visual problem
sections.copy: Clarify what the project needs to communicate, how official / strange / collectible / direct it should feel, and where it must appear.

sections.heading: 2. Build the system
sections.copy: Create the visual grammar: layout rules, typography, colors, identifiers, data fields, edition logic, print constraints, and variation rules.

sections.heading: 3. Generate the family
sections.copy: Apply the system across the required outputs while keeping each object coherent with the whole.

sections.heading: 4. Proof the real production context
sections.copy: Test size, printing, sequencing, front/back registration, readability, and output behavior—not just a screen mockup.

sections.heading: 5. Extend or hand off
sections.copy: Where appropriate, adapt the system into a reusable workflow, campaign framework, or integration.

about_page.positioning: Artist/designer and visual systems builder with traditional graphic-design and illustrative grounding, developed through extensive self-directed production work.
suggested_copy: I work between graphic design, publication design, print production, generative systems, and campaign architecture.

A large part of the practice is concerned with what happens after the first piece is designed: how the same visual logic can generate a family of related objects without flattening them into templates.
The work often uses LaTeX, TikZ, scripting, structured data, print-production constraints, and custom visual rules alongside conventional design judgment.
I am especially interested in projects where identity, rarity, sequencing, public presentation, and production logic are part of the concept—not just decoration.
do_not_overemphasize: software stack as a substitute for artistic judgment
a long list of commodity design services

contact_page.headline: Tell me what the project needs to become.
contact_page.intro: Useful inquiries describe the project, audience, timing, desired outputs, and what makes the work unusual or important.
contact_page.note: Do not use wording that promises acceptance of every inquiry. The practice is selective.

visual_direction.principle: The site should be visually controlled and editorial, but the projects—not website chrome—should carry the loudest visual energy.
site_chrome: neutral enough to support highly varied project imagery
visual_direction.signature_policy: Keep cbenton.art / CBenton as a quiet maker identity. Do not stamp the domain prominently over portfolio work unless it is part of the original artifact.

copy_style: specific descriptions of what systems do
explain technical mechanisms only when they support the visual idea
avoid repeating 'unique' and 'innovative' when a concrete mechanism can be named instead

phase_1_audit: Inspect framework, routing, component structure, styling system, content source, image pipeline, and deployment configuration before changing architecture.
Inventory every existing route and identify dead, placeholder, duplicated, or thin pages.
Find all current pricing copy and preserve any approved numeric prices before restructuring.
Find all current project images and metadata before renaming or moving assets.
Do not delete source assets simply because they are not yet used on the homepage.
Identify whether content is hard-coded, markdown/MDX, JSON, CMS-driven, or component-local.
phase_2_content_model: Create a project data model that can represent systems, not just images.
Prefer structured project metadata stored in JSON/TS/MDX frontmatter rather than duplicating copy across components.
Allow multiple images, captions, output types, rules, technologies, variable fields, and case-study sections per project.
Create pricing engagement data as structured content so wording can be edited without rebuilding layout logic.
phase_3_pages: Build /work as the primary portfolio index.
Add /approach before adding unnecessary marketing pages.
Refine /about and /contact after project architecture is in place.
phase_4_design: Create a restrained global shell and let case-study imagery provide visual intensity.
Use responsive typography and generous image widths.
Keep case-study reading width controlled even when images run wide.
Use consistent caption and metadata styling.
Make comparison layouts available for front/back, before/after, or variable-unit sets.
Support both portrait and landscape artwork without aggressive cropping.
phase_5_quality: Test images for cumulative layout shift.
Ensure route metadata, canonical URLs, Open Graph metadata, and project-specific titles exist.
Run existing lint, typecheck, test, and build commands before completion.
hard_constraints: Do not invent client names, awards, testimonials, project outcomes, revenue impact, or collaborators.
Do not call experimental or speculative work commissioned client work unless repository content proves it.
Do not describe every project as AI-generated.
Do not flatten serialized or generative systems into a generic gallery.
Do not make the website brand louder than the work.
Do not delete original project assets without explicit evidence they are redundant.
Do not rewrite project-specific terminology into generic agency language.

acceptance_criteria: A first-time visitor can understand within the first screen that CBenton builds expandable visual systems rather than isolated graphics.
The homepage no longer contains starter-template language.
The portfolio is organized by projects/systems, not only by media type.
At least one case study clearly demonstrates controlled variation across multiple related outputs.
The pricing page presents project engagement types and does not read like a commodity service menu.
Pricing does not introduce invented dollar amounts.
The site supports consulting / integration / licensing inquiries without making them the only business model.
Small projects are presented as selective, not discounted by default.
The CBenton identity remains visible but subordinate to the work.
All published routes pass the repository's build and quality checks.
